title: Forgive offences
hookLine: as we forgive those who trespass against us
tomorrow: turn the other cheek. so why did Jesus talk back when struck?

cards: Some apologies arrive with a counter running: that's the third time this month. Peter wants a counter too. Lord, how often shall my brother offend against me, and I forgive him?
Till seven times? Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims, "I say not to thee, till seven times; but till seventy times seven times." Then he tells a story.
A servant owes a king ten thousand talents, a debt too huge to picture. The king orders him sold, with his family. The servant falls down and begs, and the king forgives the whole thing.
The servant walks out free, and meets a fellow servant who owes him a hundred pence.

teach.b: He grabs him by the throat: pay what thou owest. The fellow servant falls down and begs, in nearly the same words the first servant used with the king. He's thrown into prison until he pays.

teach.h: AS I HAD COMPASSION ON YOU.
teach.b: The other servants are grieved and tell the king, and the king calls the first servant back: shouldn't you have had compassion on your fellow, as I had compassion on you? That's the answer to Peter. He asked for a number.
He got back a debt too large to count, already forgiven. Catholics pray this every time they say the Our Father: forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.
That small word, as, ties the two halves together.
Right after giving the prayer in Matthew, Jesus comes back to just one of its lines: "For if you will forgive men their offences, your heavenly Father will forgive you also your offences."
Offences, in that older spelling, is today's word. Then the hard question: what if the hurt won't leave? The Catechism answers it gently.
It isn't in our power not to feel an offense, or to forget it. But a heart that offers itself to the Holy Spirit can turn injury into compassion, and the hurt into prayer for the one who caused it.
It can begin with a prayer, while the feeling catches up later.

how: Catholics pray the Our Father daily and at every Mass, asking to be forgiven as they forgive, and seek and receive forgiveness in the sacrament of reconciliation.

o: wait for an apology, then move on
let go of what someone owes you

games.q: who's in the story — tap the pairs.
p: forgave a debt too huge to picture

s: forgiving someone means forgetting what they did
the Catechism says it isn't in our power to forget an offense. forgiveness turns the hurt into prayer.
the forgiven servant forgave his fellow servant's small debt
he grabbed him by the throat and had him thrown into prison.
the Our Father ties our forgiveness to how we forgive others
as we forgive: Jesus comes back to that line right after the prayer.

games.q: your best friend shared something you told her in confidence. she apologized, you said it's fine, and two weeks later it still stings. what fits today?
o: keep praying for her and don't hold it over her, while it heals.
admit you never forgave her, since it still hurts, and take it back.
forget it happened; real forgiveness means the memory goes away.
games.why: the Catechism says it isn't in our power not to feel or forget an offense. forgiveness can turn the hurt into prayer for her.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees in two loose fists, and let one name come to mind, someone who owes you an apology. Slowly open your hands, palms up, without forcing any feeling, the way the king opened his hand on a debt.
If you pray, you can say the line as we forgive those who trespass against us, and mean it as far as you can today.

wordCard.voice: Forgive offences. Let go of what someone owes you, the way you hope to be let go.

orig.note: Greek: forgive, let go. the verb in the Our Father, Matthew 6:12.

carryVoice: Your line: as we forgive. One small word holds the whole prayer together. Be well.
